terms.grammar: temperāre with the ablative of what is mixed in: melle, saccharō
evidence: Plin. NH 14.114: acētum melle (Lewis & Short s.v. temperō)
terms.comment: Latin says it with temperāre, to mix in due measure, and the ablative of the sweetener: Pliny tempers vinegar with honey, and Apicius ends recipe after recipe with melle temperābis. With sugar, saccharō temperāre, an ordinary combination; see the examples. The one-word verbs for “sweeten” are late or Christian (Lewis & Short).
Late Latin (Jerome, the Vulgate); classical Latin uses temperāre.

phrases.latin: Sūcus citreī nimis acidus est; paulum melle temperā.
phrases.english: The lemon juice is too sour; sweeten it with a little honey.
We’ll sweeten the cream with sugar.

phrases.latin: Similiter, ut suprā, et dē violā violācium faciēs, et eōdem modō melle temperābis.
phrases.english: Likewise, as above, you will make violet wine from violets, and sweeten it with honey in the same way.

sources: Lewis & Short: tempero · Lewis & Short: dulcoro
